Core: Atoms consist of a nucleus and electrons described by quantum-mechanical states; chemistry connects structure to observable properties. Effect: Bonding and reactivity depend on electron structure. Example: Compare carbon isotopes with the same atomic number but different neutron counts. Counterexample: An isotope is not a different element when proton number is unchanged. Common misconception: Atomic number is proton count, not total nucleon count. Calculation: For an isotope, mass number A = Z + N. Practical situation: Use periodic-table data and distinguish atomic number from mass number. Evidence: OpenStax Chemistry 2e covers atomic structure and periodic relationships

Core: Chemical bonding describes interactions that lower or organize the energy of atoms and molecules. Effect: Bond type and geometry influence melting point, solubility, conductivity and reactivity. Example: NaCl behaves differently from molecular sugar because their bonding/structures differ. Counterexample: Covalent does not automatically mean nonpolar. Common misconception: Ionic compounds are not simply “molecules of ions”; their lattice structure matters. Calculation: Formal charge bookkeeping can test a Lewis structure. Practical situation: Explain bonding without treating simple labels as absolute categories. Evidence: OpenStax Chemistry 2e provides chemical bonding and structure frameworks

Core: Stoichiometry relates quantities of reactants and products through a balanced chemical equation. Effect: It enables prediction of required reactant or expected product amounts. Example: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O gives a 2:1 mole ratio for H2:O2. Counterexample: A coefficient is not the same as a subscript. Common misconception: Moles are not grams; conversion requires molar mass. Calculation: n = m/M; use equation coefficients for mole ratios. Practical situation: Check units at every conversion step. Evidence: OpenStax Chemistry 2e quantitative chapters support mole and reaction calculations

Core: Chemical kinetics studies reaction rates and factors that influence them. Effect: Changing rate does not necessarily change equilibrium composition. Example: A catalyst can lower activation energy for an alternative pathway. Counterexample: A catalyst does not create energy or guarantee a favorable reaction. Common misconception: Faster reaction does not mean more product at equilibrium. Calculation: Rate laws are determined experimentally for a reaction. Practical situation: Do not infer a rate law solely from the balanced equation unless justified. Evidence: OpenStax Chemistry covers kinetics and mechanisms

Core: Chemical equilibrium is a dynamic state where forward and reverse reaction rates are equal. Effect: Changing conditions can shift composition until a new equilibrium is established. Example: Adding a reactant can shift a system toward products in appropriate cases. Counterexample: Equilibrium does not mean equal concentrations of reactants and products. Common misconception: Equilibrium is not a stopped reaction. Calculation: K expressions follow stoichiometric exponents in the balanced equation. Practical situation: State temperature and reaction when interpreting K. Evidence: OpenStax explicitly describes dynamic equilibrium and equilibrium calculations

Core: Acid-base chemistry concerns proton transfer, electron-pair interactions and related equilibrium models. Effect: Buffers resist pH change over a useful range but have finite capacity. Example: A weak acid can have a strong effect when concentrated enough; strength and concentration differ. Counterexample: Weak acid does not mean harmless or always dilute. Common misconception: pH is logarithmic, not a linear concentration scale. Calculation: pH = -log10(a_H+) in the idealized aqueous treatment. Practical situation: Do not use pH alone to diagnose health conditions. Evidence: OpenStax Chemistry provides acid-base and equilibrium foundations

Core: Organic chemistry studies carbon-containing molecular structures, reactions and properties. Effect: Small structural changes can change physical and chemical properties. Example: Ethanol and dimethyl ether have the same formula but different connectivity and properties. Counterexample: Same molecular formula does not guarantee same compound. Common misconception: “Organic” does not mean natural or safe. Calculation: Molecular formulas can be checked against atom counts; structure requires connectivity information. Practical situation: Avoid safety claims based solely on the word organic. Evidence: OpenStax Chemistry includes organic chemistry and functional-group foundations

Core: Chemical thermodynamics relates energy, heat, work, entropy and free energy to physical and chemical change. Effect: A negative ΔG indicates thermodynamic favorability in the stated convention, not reaction speed. Example: A process can be spontaneous yet slow. Counterexample: Spontaneous does not mean instantaneous. Common misconception: ΔG<0 is not a statement that a process is fast. Calculation: Under common constant-T,P conditions, ΔG = ΔH - TΔS. Practical situation: State conditions and distinguish thermodynamics from kinetics. Evidence: OpenStax Chemistry 2e covers entropy, laws of thermodynamics and free energy

Core: Chemistry calculations connect symbolic equations to measurable quantities with dimensional analysis. Effect: Dimensional errors can reveal incorrect setup even when arithmetic is correct. Example: For molarity, c = n/V when n is moles and V is liters. Counterexample: A numerical answer without units is incomplete in physical chemistry. Common misconception: Molarity and molality are not interchangeable. Calculation: c1V1 = c2V2 applies to simple dilution assumptions. Practical situation: Track units and assumptions explicitly. Evidence: OpenStax Chemistry quantitative chapters support these calculation frameworks

Core: Cells are basic organizational units of life with specialized structures performing coordinated functions. Effect: Membrane properties regulate exchange with the environment. Example: Mitochondria and chloroplasts illustrate specialized cellular roles. Counterexample: Not all cells have a nucleus; prokaryotic cells differ. Common misconception: “Cell = tiny bag” misses regulated internal organization. Calculation: Diffusion rate depends on gradients and physical conditions rather than a single universal number. Practical situation: Use microscopy/diagram context and distinguish prokaryotic and eukaryotic organization. Evidence: OpenStax Biology 2e provides cell structure and function foundations

Core: Cell membranes regulate movement of substances through selective permeability and transport mechanisms. Effect: Transport affects cell volume, ion balance and signaling. Example: Water can move across membranes by osmosis. Counterexample: Osmosis is not simply “water always moves to salt”; membrane and solute conditions matter. Common misconception: Active transport is not synonymous with all protein-mediated transport. Calculation: Flux depends on gradients, permeability and transport properties. Practical situation: Describe the membrane and relevant solute before predicting direction. Evidence: OpenStax Biology 2e covers membrane structure and transport

Core: Genetics studies inheritance and variation through genes, genomes and their expression. Effect: Variants can alter traits, but phenotype can also depend on environment and regulation. Example: A genotype can contribute to a phenotype without uniquely determining it. Counterexample: A gene is not identical to a visible trait. Common misconception: “Dominant” does not mean better, more common or more powerful. Calculation: Punnett-square probabilities apply only under stated inheritance assumptions. Practical situation: Separate population frequency, dominance and phenotype. Evidence: OpenStax Biology 2e provides genetics and inheritance foundations

Core: Evolution is change in heritable characteristics of populations across generations. Effect: Population frequencies can change through selection, drift, mutation and gene flow. Example: Genetic drift can change allele frequencies even without adaptive advantage. Counterexample: Individuals do not evolve genetically because they “need” to. Common misconception: Evolution is not a ladder toward perfection. Calculation: Allele-frequency change can be calculated from population counts under defined models. Practical situation: Distinguish individual adaptation during life from population evolution across generations. Evidence: OpenStax Biology 2e covers evolution, natural selection and population genetics

Core: Ecology studies interactions among organisms and their physical environment across levels of organization. Effect: Changes to one component can propagate through food webs and nutrient cycles. Example: Removing a key predator can alter prey and vegetation patterns. Counterexample: A food chain is not the whole ecosystem. Common misconception: Energy flow and matter cycling are different concepts. Calculation: Population growth models depend on assumptions and parameters. Practical situation: Use system boundaries and distinguish energy transfer from nutrient recycling. Evidence: OpenStax Biology 2e covers ecology and ecosystem processes

Core: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy and supports carbon fixation in photosynthetic organisms. Effect: Photosynthesis links energy flow with atmospheric carbon cycling. Example: Plants use light, water and CO2 to synthesize carbohydrates while releasing oxygen in oxygenic photosynthesis. Counterexample: Plants do not obtain all of their food directly from soil. Common misconception: Photosynthesis is not simply “plants breathe in CO2 and make oxygen”; it is a coupled biochemical system. Calculation: Simplified overall equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O + light -> C6H12O6 + 6O2. Practical situation: Use simplified equations as summaries, not full mechanisms. Evidence: OpenStax Biology 2e covers photosynthesis and cellular energy

Core: Cellular respiration is a set of pathways that transfer chemical energy from fuels into ATP and other useful intermediates. Effect: ATP availability supports many cellular processes. Example: Glucose can be metabolized through glycolysis; downstream pathways depend on conditions. Counterexample: Respiration is not identical to breathing. Common misconception: Anaerobic fermentation is not simply “no metabolism.” Calculation: ATP yield depends on organism, pathway and accounting assumptions. Practical situation: Avoid presenting one fixed ATP number as universal. Evidence: OpenStax Biology 2e covers cellular respiration and fermentation

Core: Biological measurements require operational definitions, controls, uncertainty awareness and appropriate sampling. Effect: Poor sampling or confounding can produce misleading conclusions. Example: A controlled experiment changes one target factor while monitoring outcomes. Counterexample: Correlation alone does not establish causation. Common misconception: A statistically significant result is not automatically biologically important. Calculation: Mean, variance and confidence intervals summarize data under assumptions. Practical situation: Record units, sample size and measurement method. Evidence: OpenStax Biology emphasizes experimental methods and scientific reasoning

Core: Health is influenced by biological, behavioral, environmental and social factors, while health systems organize prevention, treatment and care. Effect: System capacity and access affect population health. Example: Vaccination is a preventive intervention; diagnosis and treatment are different steps. Counterexample: A chatbot cannot replace a clinician or health system. Common misconception: “Healthy” cannot be inferred from one symptom or measurement alone. Calculation: Risk is often probabilistic rather than deterministic. Practical situation: For symptoms or treatment decisions, defer to qualified professionals and current clinical guidance. Evidence: WHO health topics frame health across diseases, interventions, systems and determinants. . safety: Educational only; no diagnosis, individualized prescription or dosing. Use current official clinical guidance

Core: Medicines are regulated products used to prevent, treat or lessen disease effects, with benefits and risks that depend on context. Effect: Quality and correct use influence safety and effectiveness. Example: WHO emphasizes safe, effective, quality-assured medicines and regulation. Counterexample: A medicine being available does not make it appropriate for every person. Common misconception: Natural does not mean automatically safe; prescription status does not mean “dangerous” by definition. Calculation: Dose calculations require drug-specific, patient-specific and clinical assumptions. Practical situation: Do not provide individualized prescribing or dosing; use official guidance and clinicians. Evidence: WHO medicines guidance emphasizes quality, safety, effectiveness and regulation. . safety: Educational only; no diagnosis, individualized prescription or dosing. Use current official clinical guidance

Core: Vaccination trains immune defenses to reduce the risk and severity of specified infections. Effect: High coverage can reduce transmission for some infections while individual protection varies. Example: WHO states immunization prevents millions of deaths annually and is a key primary-health intervention. Counterexample: No vaccine gives absolute protection against every outcome. Common misconception: Vaccines are not identical to antibiotics and do not work by treating bacterial infections after the fact. Calculation: Effectiveness is measured under defined populations and outcomes; do not convert population estimates into personal certainty. Practical situation: Use national immunization schedules and clinician advice. Evidence: WHO vaccines and immunization guidance. . safety: Educational only; no diagnosis, individualized prescription or dosing. Use current official clinical guidance

Core: Antimicrobial resistance occurs when microorganisms no longer respond adequately to medicines that once controlled them. Effect: AMR increases treatment difficulty and risks of severe outcomes. Example: WHO describes AMR as a major global health threat and emphasizes coordinated action. Counterexample: AMR is not the same as the body becoming “immune” to an antibiotic. Common misconception: Antibiotics do not treat viral infections such as uncomplicated influenza. Calculation: Population-level AMR metrics cannot determine which drug will work for an individual. Practical situation: Never recommend self-starting or stopping antimicrobials; consult a clinician. Evidence: WHO AMR topic and 2026 fact sheet. . safety: Educational only; no diagnosis, individualized prescription or dosing. Use current official clinical guidance

Core: Public health protects and improves population health through surveillance, prevention, policy and community interventions. Effect: Effective interventions can reduce exposure and disease burden at scale. Example: Vaccination programs and outbreak surveillance are public-health examples. Counterexample: Public health is not simply hospital medicine at a larger scale. Common misconception: A population statistic does not automatically predict an individual outcome. Calculation: Rates and risks require a defined population, period and denominator. Practical situation: Use current official health agencies for outbreaks and rapidly changing guidance. Evidence: WHO health-topic framework and immunization/AMR guidance. . safety: Educational only; no diagnosis, individualized prescription or dosing. Use current official clinical guidance

Core: Diagnosis is a clinical process that integrates history, examination, tests and differential reasoning to identify a condition. Effect: Context and testing can change the differential substantially. Example: Fever can occur in many conditions, so fever alone is not a diagnosis. Counterexample: An online answer cannot establish a diagnosis without clinical evaluation. Common misconception: “One symptom = one disease” is unsafe reasoning. Calculation: Diagnostic tests have sensitivity, specificity and predictive values that depend on context. Practical situation: FINZANJIR AI should explain educationally and recommend professional care when appropriate. Evidence: WHO health topics demonstrate the breadth of conditions and interventions requiring context. . safety: Educational only; no diagnosis, individualized prescription or dosing. Use current official clinical guidance

Core: Mental health concerns involve emotional, cognitive and behavioral well-being and may require professional assessment. Effect: Support, early help and appropriate care can improve outcomes. Example: WHO lists mental health among major health topics. Counterexample: A chatbot should not label a person with a psychiatric diagnosis from a conversation. Common misconception: A difficult day is not automatically a disorder. Calculation: Screening scores are not equivalent to diagnosis. Practical situation: Use supportive language and urgent local help when safety risk is present. Evidence: WHO health-topic framework supports a broad, non-diagnostic approach. . safety: Educational only; no diagnosis, individualized prescription or dosing. Use current official clinical guidance

Core: Medical evidence links claims to studies, guidelines, surveillance and clinical context with varying certainty. Effect: Strong evidence can still have limits in populations or outcomes. Example: A randomized trial and an observational association answer different questions. Counterexample: One headline study is not automatically the final word. Common misconception: “Published” does not mean “proven.” Calculation: Effect size, uncertainty intervals and study design matter. Practical situation: Prefer current authoritative guidelines and multiple high-quality sources for high-stakes claims. Evidence: WHO pages illustrate the need for current, regulated health information. . safety: Educational only; no diagnosis, individualized prescription or dosing. Use current official clinical guidance

Core: The Solar System consists of the Sun and objects gravitationally bound to it, including eight planets, dwarf planets, moons and smaller bodies. Effect: Different regions favor different compositions and planetary types. Example: Inner planets are rocky; outer giant planets are gas/ice giants. Counterexample: Pluto is classified as a dwarf planet under the IAU definition. Common misconception: The Solar System is not the same thing as the Milky Way. Calculation: Orbital periods can be related to distance and central mass under Keplerian approximations. Practical situation: Use current NASA/IAU definitions for classification. Evidence: NASA Solar System facts and exploration pages

Core: Exoplanets are planets beyond our Solar System detected and characterized through astronomical measurements. Effect: Different methods have different biases and detection limits. Example: Transit observations can reveal periodic dips in a star’s brightness. Counterexample: A detected exoplanet is not automatically habitable. Common misconception: Earth-sized does not mean Earth-like. Calculation: Transit depth roughly relates to the squared planet-to-star radius ratio under simple assumptions. Practical situation: Separate confirmed detection from candidate status and habitability claims. Evidence: NASA exoplanet resources describe multiple detection methods and diverse planet types

Core: Stars are self-gravitating luminous objects whose structure and evolution depend strongly on mass and composition. Effect: Stars create and distribute many heavy elements over cosmic history. Example: NASA describes stars as fundamental building blocks of galaxies and discusses stellar populations. Counterexample: All stars do not have the same lifetime or final state. Common misconception: Brightness alone does not uniquely determine mass. Calculation: Luminosity, flux and distance are linked by inverse-square behavior in simple isotropic cases. Practical situation: Use observed quantities with uncertainty and distance assumptions. Evidence: NASA star/exoplanet science resources

Core: A galaxy is a gravitationally bound system containing stars, gas, dust, dark matter and other components. Effect: Galaxy properties change over cosmic time. Example: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy according to NASA. Counterexample: A galaxy is not a single star system like the Solar System. Common misconception: “All galaxies look like spirals” is false. Calculation: Angular size and physical size require distance information. Practical situation: Distinguish observational classification from speculative interpretation. Evidence: NASA Solar System/galaxy educational resources

Core: Orbital motion results from gravity and initial motion, producing trajectories that can be approximately Keplerian in suitable systems. Effect: Changing energy or angular momentum changes orbital properties. Example: Earth remains in orbit because its tangential motion and solar gravity combine into a trajectory. Counterexample: Orbit does not mean gravity is absent. Common misconception: Astronauts are not “outside gravity”; they are in free fall. Calculation: For a circular orbit, v=sqrt(GM/r) under a point-mass approximation. Practical situation: State the two-body/circular-orbit assumptions. Evidence: NASA basic space-flight and Solar System resources

Core: Cosmology studies the universe on the largest scales, including its expansion, composition and history. Effect: Models can be updated when new observations challenge parameters or assumptions. Example: Galaxy redshift can provide evidence related to cosmic expansion in appropriate contexts. Counterexample: Cosmology is not the same as astrology. Common misconception: A model is not identical to a direct photograph of the entire universe. Calculation: Distances and redshifts require cosmological model assumptions for interpretation. Practical situation: Separate established observations from model-dependent inference. Evidence: NASA educational resources provide large-scale cosmic context

Core: Astrobiology and the search for life examine environments, biosignatures and planetary conditions that could support life. Effect: A potentially habitable environment is not proof of life. Example: NASA states that Earth is currently the only place where life is known. Counterexample: An atmospheric molecule alone may have non-biological sources. Common misconception: “Habitable” means potentially suitable, not inhabited. Calculation: Probability claims require explicit assumptions and base rates. Practical situation: Present uncertain life claims as hypotheses until evidence supports them. Evidence: NASA search-for-life and exoplanet resources

Core: Astronomical knowledge is built from light, timing, spectra, motion and statistical inference because direct sampling is usually impossible. Effect: Uncertainty determines how strongly a conclusion can be stated. Example: Parallax can estimate nearby stellar distances. Counterexample: A colorful telescope image is not necessarily a direct-color photograph. Common misconception: A measured signal is not automatically a confirmed interpretation. Calculation: Parallax distance uses d proportional to 1/p under defined units. Practical situation: Report uncertainty and method with astronomical measurements. Evidence: NASA exoplanet and solar-system science pages illustrate observation methods

Core: Plate tectonics describes large lithospheric plates moving relative to one another. Effect: Long-term plate motion reshapes Earth’s surface. Example: Convergent boundaries can include subduction. Counterexample: Earthquakes occur only at plate boundaries is too absolute. Common misconception: Plate tectonics is not the same as continental drift alone. Calculation: Plate velocity can be estimated from distance/time measurements. Practical situation: Use boundary type and local geology when interpreting hazards. Evidence: USGS explains plate tectonics and its relation to earthquakes and volcanoes

Core: Earthquakes are sudden releases of stored elastic energy associated with fault rupture and ground motion. Effect: Ground shaking can damage structures and trigger secondary hazards. Example: USGS monitors earthquakes and assesses hazards. Counterexample: Magnitude and intensity are not identical concepts. Common misconception: An earthquake cannot be predicted exactly from a simple calendar pattern. Calculation: Magnitude scales are logarithmic; do not treat increments as linear energy changes. Practical situation: Follow local seismic safety guidance; do not claim exact prediction. Evidence: USGS earthquake hazard resources

Core: Volcanoes are openings or structures through which magma, gases and volcanic material reach the surface or near-surface environment. Effect: Eruptions can produce lava, ash, gases and secondary hazards. Example: Volcanic hazards vary by volcano and eruption type. Counterexample: All volcanoes do not erupt explosively. Common misconception: Volcanoes are not simply “mountains that spit fire.” Calculation: Hazard probability is location- and time-dependent. Practical situation: Use official observatory alerts for real hazards. Evidence: USGS earth-science and hazard-monitoring framework

Core: The water cycle describes continuous movement of water among atmosphere, land, oceans, ice and living systems. Effect: Changes in precipitation, storage or use affect water availability. Example: Rainfall can feed rivers, soil moisture and groundwater depending on conditions. Counterexample: Water does not simply move from ocean to cloud to river in one fixed path. Common misconception: The water cycle is a closed global cycle with no local water-management issues is misleading. Calculation: Water balance can be expressed as inputs minus outputs plus storage change. Practical situation: Define watershed and time period before calculating balance. Evidence: USGS water resources and National Geographic water-map resources

Core: Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions; climate describes longer-term patterns and variability. Effect: Climate trends do not determine every individual day. Example: A cold day does not by itself refute long-term warming. Counterexample: Weather and climate are not synonyms. Common misconception: One measurement is insufficient to establish a climate trend. Calculation: Trend estimation requires defined period, data quality and statistical treatment. Practical situation: Use long-term datasets for climate claims. Evidence: National Geographic climate mapping and Earth-science resources

Core: Geohazards are natural Earth processes that can harm people or infrastructure, including earthquakes, landslides, volcanoes and floods. Effect: Preparedness and resilient design can reduce impacts. Example: Building codes can reduce earthquake losses even though they cannot stop earthquakes. Counterexample: Hazard is not identical to risk. Common misconception: “Natural disaster” does not mean impacts are unavoidable. Calculation: Risk can be conceptualized as a function of hazard, exposure and vulnerability; exact models vary. Practical situation: Use local hazard maps and official alerts. Evidence: USGS hazard monitoring and Earth-science education

Core: Earth materials include minerals, rocks, soils and sediments formed through geological processes. Effect: Material properties influence landscapes, resources and hazards. Example: The rock cycle links igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic processes. Counterexample: Rocks and minerals are not interchangeable terms. Common misconception: Soil is not simply crushed rock; it includes organic matter and biological processes. Calculation: Mineral identification can use observable properties such as hardness, streak and cleavage. Practical situation: Use multiple properties rather than color alone. Evidence: USGS Earth-science educational framework

Core: Earth science links atmosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere and biosphere as interacting systems. Effect: Feedbacks can amplify or damp changes. Example: Water, climate, land and ecosystems interact in drought and flood processes. Counterexample: Earth systems are not independent boxes. Common misconception: A single-variable explanation often misses coupled feedbacks. Calculation: System models track stocks, flows and feedbacks under assumptions. Practical situation: Make system boundaries and timescales explicit. Evidence: USGS and National Geographic Earth-system mapping resources

Core: Maps represent spatial information using symbols, scale, projection and coordinate systems. Effect: A map can simplify reality while preserving selected relationships. Example: A thematic map can show population density by region. Counterexample: A map is not the territory itself. Common misconception: Bigger visual area does not always mean larger real-world area. Calculation: Scale converts map distance to ground distance under the stated scale. Practical situation: Check projection, date, source and legend before interpreting. Evidence: National Geographic MapMaker emphasizes maps as tools for analysis and storytelling

Core: Latitude and longitude provide a global coordinate framework for locating places. Effect: Correct coordinate order and datum matter for practical GIS use. Example: A location can be specified with latitude and longitude. Counterexample: Latitude and longitude are not interchangeable. Common misconception: Degrees alone without reference direction can be ambiguous. Calculation: Distance from coordinates requires a geodesic or projection-aware method. Practical situation: Keep N/S/E/W or signed-coordinate conventions explicit. Evidence: National Geographic MapMaker includes latitude and longitude resources

Core: Physical geography studies Earth’s physical landscapes, climate, water, soils and natural processes. Effect: Climate and geology help explain spatial patterns. Example: Mountain relief influences climate and drainage. Counterexample: Physical geography is not only memorizing place names. Common misconception: One climate variable cannot explain every landscape. Calculation: Spatial comparisons require consistent units and scales. Practical situation: Use maps and multiple layers to connect processes to patterns. Evidence: National Geographic MapMaker resources span physical geography, climatology and Earth science

Core: Human geography studies spatial patterns of people, cultures, economies, migration and settlements. Effect: Patterns change over time and can differ by scale. Example: Urbanization can change land use, transport and service demand. Counterexample: Human geography is not just population counting. Common misconception: A correlation between place and outcome does not prove a single cause. Calculation: Rates require a denominator and time period. Practical situation: Distinguish descriptive spatial patterns from causal claims. Evidence: National Geographic MapMaker includes human-geography and population-related layers

Core: GIS is a system for storing, analyzing and visualizing geographically referenced data. Effect: Layering can reveal relationships not visible in a single table. Example: Overlaying land use with flood zones can support planning. Counterexample: GIS output is only as good as its data and coordinate assumptions. Common misconception: A colorful GIS map is not automatically accurate. Calculation: Spatial joins and distance calculations depend on geometry and coordinate reference systems. Practical situation: Record data source, date, resolution and projection. Evidence: National Geographic MapMaker is a GIS educational tool

Core: Climate geography examines spatial and temporal patterns of climate and their relationships with landscapes and human activity. Effect: Climate affects ecosystems, agriculture, water and settlement. Example: Precipitation maps reveal strong spatial differences. Counterexample: Climate is not identical to daily weather. Common misconception: A single city’s weather does not represent a whole climate zone. Calculation: Climate normals summarize long-term conditions; exact period must be specified. Practical situation: Use current datasets for changing climate indicators. Evidence: National Geographic climate and precipitation MapMaker resources

Core: Water geography studies the spatial distribution, movement and use of surface and groundwater. Effect: Overuse or uneven access can create water stress. Example: A watershed links upstream activities to downstream effects. Counterexample: Water scarcity is not only a lack of rainfall; demand and infrastructure matter. Common misconception: A river basin and political boundary are not the same. Calculation: Water balance compares inputs, outputs and storage over a defined period. Practical situation: Use basin-level data and current water-resource information. Evidence: National Geographic World Water Map and precipitation resources

Core: Geographic reasoning connects location, distance, scale, pattern, process and interaction to explain spatial phenomena. Effect: Changing scale can change the apparent pattern and explanation. Example: A city-level pattern may differ from a national average. Counterexample: Map correlation is not automatically causation. Common misconception: Nearest-neighbor intuition can fail in clustered systems. Calculation: Spatial statistics require assumptions and appropriate data. Practical situation: Always state geographic scale and data vintage. Evidence: National Geographic mapping resources emphasize spatial analysis and visualization

Core: Historical periodization organizes the past into analytical periods, but boundaries vary by region and scholarly tradition. Effect: Different period boundaries can emphasize different transitions. Example: Library of Congress catalogs world history across ancient, medieval and modern periods. Counterexample: There is no single universally correct periodization for every region. Common misconception: Ancient/medieval/modern labels are not identical worldwide. Calculation: Chronologies require explicit dates and regional scope. Practical situation: State region and period definition when answering history questions. Evidence: Library of Congress historical works and World History Encyclopedia period indexes

Core: Primary sources originate close to the event or subject; secondary sources interpret or synthesize evidence. Effect: Corroboration can strengthen or complicate a historical claim. Example: A contemporary letter is primary evidence for its author’s perspective, not automatic proof of every claim. Counterexample: Primary does not mean unbiased or complete. Common misconception: Secondary does not mean false; it can provide analysis and context. Calculation: Compare claims across independent sources when possible. Practical situation: Record creator, date, place, purpose and provenance. Evidence: Library of Congress digitized historical collections emphasize source metadata and rights

Core: Historical causation explains how multiple conditions, decisions and contingencies contribute to change. Effect: Separating long-term conditions from immediate triggers improves explanation. Example: An economic crisis may be a condition while a political decision acts as a trigger. Counterexample: A single-cause story can oversimplify history. Common misconception: Correlation in time does not prove causation. Calculation: Causal claims should specify mechanism and evidence. Practical situation: Use competing explanations and counterevidence. Evidence: Historical source collections support contextual and comparative analysis

Core: Chronology orders events in time and helps test whether proposed sequences are possible. Effect: Chronology can reveal anachronistic claims. Example: A policy cannot cause an event that occurred before the policy. Counterexample: Chronology alone does not establish causation. Common misconception: Earlier does not automatically mean causal. Calculation: Date intervals can be computed when calendars and conventions are explicit. Practical situation: State calendar and approximate dates where necessary. Evidence: Library of Congress and World History Encyclopedia provide period/time indexes

Core: Civilizations are complex historical societies characterized by institutions, economic systems, cultural practices and built environments. Effect: Civilizations change through internal developments and external interaction. Example: Ancient societies show diverse political and economic arrangements. Counterexample: Civilization is not a synonym for “more advanced.” Common misconception: Do not rank cultures using a single linear progress scale. Calculation: Population, trade and production estimates require source-specific assumptions. Practical situation: Avoid anachronistic categories and respect regional context. Evidence: World History Encyclopedia organizes historical topics by periods and regions; Library of Congress provides digitized historical works

Core: States and empires are political organizations whose structures, territories and legitimacy change over time. Effect: Expansion can increase resources while also increasing management costs. Example: Empires can contain diverse peoples and institutions. Counterexample: Empire is not simply a synonym for any large country. Common misconception: Military strength alone does not explain state longevity. Calculation: Historical comparisons need comparable measures and time periods. Practical situation: Distinguish state, empire, dynasty and nation where relevant. Evidence: World History Encyclopedia and Library of Congress period/subject classifications

Core: Industrialization is a transformation involving mechanized production, energy systems, labor organization, urbanization and related social change. Effect: Industrialization can increase output while creating new social and environmental problems. Example: Factory systems changed production organization and urban life in many regions. Counterexample: Industrialization did not occur identically everywhere. Common misconception: Technology alone does not explain all industrial change. Calculation: Productivity and growth measures require defined units and periods. Practical situation: Compare regions with attention to institutions and timing. Evidence: Library of Congress world-history classifications include modern history and industrial-era subjects; historical scholarship requires regional context

Core: Central Asian history includes interconnected nomadic, urban, imperial, trade, religious and cultural processes across long periods. Effect: Political and cultural boundaries changed repeatedly. Example: Silk Road networks connected multiple regions rather than one single road. Counterexample: Central Asian history is not reducible to one empire or one ethnic group. Common misconception: Modern national borders should not be projected unchanged onto ancient periods. Calculation: Historical claims need region/date/source specificity. Practical situation: Use primary-source collections and specialized regional scholarship for detailed claims. Evidence: World History Encyclopedia explicitly includes Central Asia as a regional index; LOC provides broad historical source collections

Core: Epistemology studies knowledge, justification, belief and related questions about how we know. Effect: Uncertainty can remain even after substantial evidence. Example: Distinguish “I believe” from “I know” in ordinary reasoning. Counterexample: Epistemology is not simply memorizing philosophers. Common misconception: Confidence is not the same as truth. Calculation: Bayesian updating can model belief revision under explicit probabilistic assumptions. Practical situation: Mark uncertainty and evidence source. Evidence: Stanford Encyclopedia identifies epistemology as study of knowledge and how we know

Core: Logic studies valid reasoning and the structure of arguments. Effect: Soundness additionally requires true premises under the relevant semantics. Example: A valid argument can have a false conclusion if a premise is false. Counterexample: Validity is not the same as factual truth of every statement. Common misconception: “Logical” does not mean “true.” Calculation: Formal logic uses symbolic rules to test inference structures. Practical situation: Separate argument form from factual content. Evidence: Stanford Encyclopedia discusses logic as study of valid reasoning

Core: Ethics examines questions about right action, value, responsibility and how people ought to act. Effect: Ethical conflicts may require balancing competing values. Example: A decision can be evaluated by consequences and duties in different frameworks. Counterexample: Ethics is not identical to personal preference. Common misconception: One framework does not automatically resolve every case. Calculation: Decision analysis can list stakeholders, harms, benefits and constraints without claiming a universal answer. Practical situation: State assumptions and affected parties. Evidence: Stanford Encyclopedia places ethics among core philosophical fields

Core: Metaphysics investigates fundamental questions about what exists, what kinds of things there are and how reality is structured. Effect: Different frameworks can produce competing explanations. Example: Questions about free will and mind-body relations are treated as metaphysical problems. Counterexample: Metaphysics is not simply supernatural speculation. Common misconception: A metaphysical claim can be philosophically rigorous without being experimentally settled. Calculation: Formal argument structure can clarify premises and conclusions. Practical situation: Separate empirical questions from conceptual/metaphysical ones. Evidence: Stanford Encyclopedia metaphysics overview

Core: Philosophy of science examines scientific explanation, evidence, models, inference and the limits of scientific knowledge. Effect: Models can be useful without being literal copies of reality. Example: A model may predict observations within a domain while simplifying mechanisms. Counterexample: A scientific theory is not merely a guess in the technical sense. Common misconception: One failed prediction does not always instantly falsify an entire research program. Calculation: Uncertainty and model comparison can be formalized statistically. Practical situation: Distinguish data, model, inference and conclusion. Evidence: Stanford Encyclopedia resources on epistemology/logic provide foundational reasoning concepts

Core: Epistemic logic formally represents knowledge and belief of agents and can model information states and their changes. Effect: The framework supports reasoning about multiple agents and changing information. Example: SEP gives examples such as K_a φ for agent a knowing φ. Counterexample: Knowledge and belief are not automatically interchangeable. Common misconception: A formal model is not a claim that human cognition literally works that way. Calculation: Modal semantics use possible-world structures under specified assumptions. Practical situation: Treat formal models as tools with explicit axioms. Evidence: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Epistemic Logic

Core: Phenomenology studies structures of experience and first-person phenomena while connecting to questions about consciousness and meaning. Effect: Phenomenological analysis can complement but not replace empirical methods. Example: SEP distinguishes phenomenology from ontology, epistemology, logic and ethics. Counterexample: Phenomenology is not simply “describing feelings.” Common misconception: First-person reports are evidence of experience, not automatically proof of external facts. Calculation: Formal quantification is not the defining method of phenomenology. Practical situation: Keep first-person experience distinct from external causal claims. Evidence: Stanford Encyclopedia phenomenology entry

Core: Critical reasoning evaluates claims by checking evidence, assumptions, alternatives and inference quality. Effect: Considering counterexamples reduces overconfidence. Example: A strong claim should survive reasonable alternative explanations. Counterexample: Being skeptical does not mean rejecting everything. Common misconception: More sources do not automatically mean better evidence. Calculation: Argument maps can make premise-conclusion relationships explicit. Practical situation: Ask what evidence would change the conclusion. Evidence: SEP logic and epistemology provide conceptual foundations for reasoning

FINZANJIR Fuqarolar, banklar va to‘lov infratuzilmasi uchun raqamli moliyaviy xavfsizlik platformasi Yakuniy loyiha konsepsiyasi • 14 bob • 2026 Firibgarlikni erta aniqlash • xavfni tahlil qilish • ogohlantirish • qonuniy javob • doimiy rivojlanish Muallif rasmi — loyiha dossieridagi yagona shaxsiy foto. Loyiha muallifining motivatsiyasi va ijtimoiy maqsadi FINZANJIR loyihasining paydo bo‘lishi faqat texnologik g‘oya yoki tijoriy mahsulot yaratish istagi bilan bog‘liq emas. Loyihaning asosiy motivatsiyasi real hayotda moliyaviy qiyinchiliklarga duch kelayotgan, firibgarlik, noto‘g‘ri moliyaviy qarorlar yoki yetarli moliyaviy bilimga ega bo‘lmagani sababli zarar ko‘rishi mumkin bo‘lgan insonlarga yordam berish istagidan kelib chiqadi. Muallifning fikricha, inson moliyaviy muammoga duch kelgandan keyin yordam berishdan ko‘ra, muammo chuqurlashishidan oldin xavfni aniqlash, odamni ogohlantirish va unga to‘g‘ri yo‘lni ko‘rsatish muhimroq. Shu sababli FINZANJIR nafaqat moliyaviy firibgarlikni aniqlash, balki oddiy fuqaroga ham tushunarli tarzda xavf sababini ko‘rsatish va ehtiyot choralarini tushuntirishga yo‘naltiriladi. Muallif bu loyihani odamlarni shunchaki “boy qilish” uchun yaratmayapti

xavfsizligi va savodxonligini oshirish, ularni firibgarlikdan himoya qilish, moliyaviy xatolar sabab yuzaga keladigan og‘ir oqibatlarni kamaytirish va imkon qadar odamga muammoga tushishidan oldin yordam berish. Chunki bir fuqaroning moliyaviy holati yaxshilansa, bundan uning oilasi ham foyda ko‘radi. Oilalar barqaror bo‘lsa, jamiyatning iqtisodiy va ijtimoiy barqarorligi ham kuchayadi. Shu ma’noda, FINZANJIRning uzoq muddatli maqsadi individual moliyaviy xavfsizlikdan boshlanib, kengroq ijtimoiy manfaatga xizmat qilishdir. Bu qarash O‘zbekiston Prezidenti Shavkat Mirziyoyevning 2017-yilgi BMT Bosh Assambleyasining 72-sessiyasidagi nutqida bildirilgan “xalq boy bo‘lsa, davlat ham boy va qudratli bo‘ladi” degan fikri bilan hamohangdir. Mazkur fikr FINZANJIR uchun shuni anglatadiki, aholining moliyaviy xavfsizligi, bilimlari va imkoniyatlari oshishi faqat alohida shaxsning manfaatiga emas, balki oilalar, jamiyat va mamlakatning umumiy farovonligiga ham ijobiy ta’sir qilishi mumkin. Shu sababli muallif FINZANJIRni oddiy texnologik mahsulot sifatida emas, balki insonlarning moliyaviy xavfsizligini mustahkamlashga xizmat qilishi mumkin bo‘lgan uzoq muddatli platforma sifatida tasavvur qiladi. Loyiha orqali hech kimga “100 foiz boyib ketasiz” yoki “daromadingiz kafolatlanadi” degan va’da berilmaydi

Aksincha, maqsad — odamga xavfni tushunish, to‘g‘ri qaror qabul qilish, moliyaviy firibgarlikdan himoyalanish va mavjud imkoniyatlardan oqilona foydalanish uchun texnologik vosita berishdir. Muallifning asosiy umidi shuki, agar odamlar moliyaviy jihatdan xavfsizroq, bilimliroq va imkoniyatlardan yaxshiroq foydalana oladigan bo‘lsa, bu o‘z navbatida oilalar farovonligi va jamiyat barqarorligiga ijobiy ta’sir ko‘rsatadi. Manba: O‘zbekiston Respublikasi Prezidenti Shavkat Mirziyoyevning BMT Bosh Assambleyasining 72-sessiyasidagi nutqi, 19.09.2017. Rasmiy manba: President.uz, 20.09.2017. Loyiha nomining shakllanishi: «Kiber Qalqon»dan FINZANJIRgacha Dastlabki ishchi nom sifatida «Kiber Qalqon» tushunchasi loyihaning kiberxavflardan himoyalash g‘oyasini ifodalagan. Loyiha rivojlanishi bilan vazifa faqat bitta himoya qatlamidan iborat emasligi, balki fuqaro → ilova → risk tahlili → bank/to‘lov tashkiloti → hodisadan keyingi javob kabi uzluksiz moliyaviy xavfsizlik zanjirini qamrab olishi aniqroq shakllandi. Shu sababli loyiha nomi «FINZANJIR»ga o‘zgartirildi. «FIN» moliyaviy yo‘nalishni, «ZANJIR» esa xavfni aniqlashdan boshlab ogohlantirish, tekshiruv, vakolatli javob va keyingi tiklashgacha bo‘lgan bog‘langan jarayonlar tizimini anglatadi. «Kiber Qalqon» davridagi himoya, xavfni aniqlash va kiberxavfsizlik g‘oyalari FINZANJIRning poydevori sifatida saqlangan

ni ham ko‘rsatishi kerak: masalan, noodatiy vaqt, yuqori takroriylik, yangi qabul qiluvchi, qurilma/sessiya anomaliyasi yoki zanjirdagi ketma-ket xavf signallari. AI Security: Prompt Injection, Sensitive Data va Output Control AI qatlamida foydalanuvchi kiritgan matn avtomatik ravishda ishonchli ko‘rsatma sifatida qabul qilinmasligi kerak. Kelajakdagi arxitekturada foydalanuvchi inputi Topic Routerga yo‘naltirilishidan oldin xavfsizlik tekshiruvlaridan o‘tkaziladi. Kelajakdagi himoya zanjiri: [User Input] → [Input Normalization] → [Prompt/Instruction Injection Check] → [Authorization/Context Check] → [Topic Router] → [Knowledge Retrieval] → [Answer Generation/Selection] → [Sensitive Data Check] → [Safety Check] → [Audit] → [Response/Safe Fallback] AI hech qachon OTP, CVV/CVC, parol yoki boshqa maxfiy autentifikatsiya ma’lumotlarini so‘rashga yo‘naltirilmasligi kerak. Agar savol xavfsiz javob doirasidan chiqsa, tizim Safe Fallback orqali xavfsiz va cheklangan javob beradi. - Joriy APKdagi bilim qatlamining mavjudligi Production darajasidagi AI Security nazoratlari joriy qilinganini anglatmaydi. - Prompt injection, output validation va sensitive-data filtering MVP/Pilot uchun alohida acceptance criteria sifatida tekshiriladi. - AI xavfsizlik nazoratlari test, monitoring, audit va zarur hollarda rollback imkoniyatlari bilan bog‘lanadi

FINZANJIR AI qatlami loyiha doirasidagi bilim va yo‘naltirish mexanizmi sifatida qaraladi. U umumiy maqsadli chatbot sifatida barcha savollarga 100% javob berishni kafolatlamaydi. Bilim bazasi cheklangan bo‘lib, javob faqat mavjud bilim, tasdiqlangan loyiha qoidalari va xavfsiz fallback mexanizmi doirasida shakllantiriladi. Joriy holatda – APKda AI savol-javob interfeysi va demonstratsion bilimga asoslangan javob oqimi mavjud. Biroq real generativ model/API, bank ma’lumotlari bilan real-time integratsiya, Production darajasidagi model monitoringi va to‘liq avtomatik Knowledge Base orchestration mavjud deb ko‘rsatilmaydi. Bular keyingi MVP/Pilot/Production rivojlanish yo‘nalishlaridir. 7-chizma. AI Knowledge + Safety Flow. 4.7. Kelajakdagi 24/7 avtomatik monitoring va inson aralashuvi chegarasi FINZANJIRning kelajakdagi bank/PSP bilan integratsiyalashgan arxitekturasi har bir tranzaksiyani inson tomonidan qo‘lda ko‘rib chiqishga emas, ruxsat etilgan ma’lumot va xavf signallarini avtomatik baholashga tayanadi. Bu “odam barcha tranzaksiyalarni ko‘rib turadi” degani emas. Avtomatik baholashda tranzaksiya summasi yagona mezon bo‘lmaydi. Tizim vaqt, takroriylik, yuboruvchi va qabul qiluvchi bilan bog‘liq ruxsat etilgan signallar, qurilma/IP/sessiya anomaliyalari, tranzaksiyalar ketma-ketligi va boshqa tasdiqlangan indikatorlarni birgalikda baholashi mumkin

Misol: A bankdagi fuqaroning mablag‘i B bankka, undan C bankka va keyin D hisobiga o‘tsa, bitta bank ushbu zanjirning faqat o‘ziga tegishli qismini ko‘rishi mumkin. Qonuniy Data Exchange va tegishli integratsiya mavjud bo‘lsa, FINZANJIR turli tashkilotlardan kelgan ruxsat etilgan xavf signallarini birlashtirib, zanjirni kengroq tahlil qilishi mumkin. Past xavfli holatlarda avtomatik monitoring davom etadi. O‘rta xavfda kelajakdagi tizim avtomatik Case yaratib REVIEW holatiga yo‘naltirishi mumkin. Yuqori xavfda esa vakolat va bank/PSP qoidalariga muvofiq qo‘shimcha tasdiqlash, vaqtincha himoya, xabarnoma yoki eskalatsiya jarayoni ishga tushirilishi mumkin. Avtomatik Case ochilishi firibgarlik bo‘yicha yakuniy huquqiy hukm hisoblanmaydi. Ushbu imkoniyat hozirgi – APKning mavjud funksiyasi emas; u MVP/Pilot/Production bosqichlarida huquqiy, texnik va xavfsizlik talablaridan keyin ishlab chiqiladigan kelajakdagi arxitektura sifatida belgilanadi. 4.8. Integratsiya ma’lumotlari sifati va texnik barqarorlik API/data contract nazorati: har bir integratsiya uchun schema, majburiy va ixtiyoriy maydonlar, identifikatorlar, timestamp/timezone, versiya, validation, error code, timeout, retry, idempotency, rate limit va audit talablari yozma ravishda belgilanadi. Schema o‘zgarganda backward compatibility yoki migration rejasi va test dalili talab qilinadi

Data quality uchun completeness, validity, consistency, timeliness va duplication ko‘rsatkichlari alohida kuzatiladi. Noto‘liq yoki shubhali ma’lumot xavf modeliga avtomatik ravishda ishonchli signal sifatida kiritilmasligi, zarur bo‘lsa data-quality flag bilan belgilanishi kerak. Bank va PSP tizimlari turli format, maydon nomlari, vaqt tamg‘alari yoki javob tezligidan foydalanishi mumkin. Shu sababli kelajakdagi Data Exchange qatlamida schema/data standard, validation, normalization, duplicate detection, timestamp tekshiruvi, retry, timeout, idempotency va audit mexanizmlari ko‘zda tutiladi. Ma’lumot to‘liq yoki vaqtida kelmasa, bu holat alohida texnik signal sifatida qayd etilib, risk baholashning cheklanganligi ko‘rsatilishi kerak. API uzilishi, kechikkan yoki to‘liq bo‘lmagan ma’lumot, FINZANJIR xizmatidagi uzilish yoki bank javobining kelmasligi kabi holatlar uchun monitoring, retry/fallback, incident response, backup va DR/BCP mexanizmlari bo‘lishi kerak. Bu holatlarda tizim mavjud bo‘lmagan ma’lumotni taxmin qilib to‘ldirmaydi. 4.9. Rollar va kirish huquqlarini boshqarish RACI tamoyili: har bir kritik jarayon uchun Responsible (bajaruvchi), Accountable (yakuniy javobgar), Consulted (maslahatchi) va Informed (xabardor qilinuvchi) rollari belgilanadi

Ayniqsa Risk Rule/Model o‘zgarishi, Case escalation, Production release, ma’lumotga kirish va incident response jarayonlarida bir kishiga barcha vakolatlarni jamlashga yo‘l qo‘yilmasligi kerak. Least privilege, separation of duties va privileged access nazorati Production qabulining alohida sharti bo‘ladi. Prototipdagi rol ko‘rinishi bunday korporativ IAM/PAM nazoratlari amalda to‘liq ishlayotganini anglatmaydi. Kelajakdagi platformada fuqaro, bank operatori, FINZANJIR operatori, xavfsizlik mutaxassisi, administrator hamda audit/compliance kabi rollar uchun alohida kirish chegaralari belgilanadi. Role-Based Access, MFA/PAM, least privilege, access review va audit loglari orqali hech bir rolga zarur bo‘lmagan ma’lumotga teng darajada kirish berilmaydi. 4.10. Risk modeli, bilim bazasi va versiya boshqaruvi FINZANJIRda risk indikatorlari, risk qoidalari/modeli, Knowledge Base va ular bilan bog‘liq konfiguratsiyalar nazorat qilinadigan va versiyalanadigan obyektlar sifatida boshqarilishi kerak. Maqsad — tizimda qaysi qoida, indikator yoki bilim bazasi versiyasi qachon va qanday o‘zgarganini aniqlash hamda zarur bo‘lsa oldingi holatga qaytish imkoniyatini ta’minlash

i → Knowledge Base → Version → Test → Approval → Release → Monitoring → Feedback → Recalibration/Rollback Versiya boshqaruvi kamida quyidagi obyektlarni qamrab olishi mumkin: - risk indikatorlari; - risk qoidalari va parametrlar; - risk modeli yoki model konfiguratsiyasi; - Knowledge Base tarkibi; - Topic Router qoidalari; - AI xavfsizlik qoidalari; - Case routing va tegishli konfiguratsiyalar; - API/schema o‘zgarishlari; - tizim konfiguratsiyalari; - tegishli hujjatlar va yo‘riqnomalar. Har bir muhim o‘zgarishda quyidagi ma’lumotlar qayd etilishi maqsadga muvofiq: Nazorat elementi| Qayd etiladigan ma’lumot Version| Versiya raqami yoki identifikatori Change| Nima o‘zgargani Reason| O‘zgarish sababi Source| O‘zgarishga asos bo‘lgan manba yoki dalil Owner| Mas’ul rol Test| Qaysi testlardan o‘tkazilgani Approval| Kim tomonidan tasdiqlangani Release| Qachon joriy etilgani Monitoring| Joriy etilgandan keyingi kuzatuv Rollback| Zarur bo‘lsa oldingi versiyaga qaytish rejasi Risk modeli yoki indikator o‘zgartirilganda uning FP/FN ko‘rsatkichlariga, Case oqimiga, AI javoblariga va boshqa bog‘liq jarayonlarga ta’siri ham baholanishi kerak. Knowledge Base yangilanganda esa yangi bilim yoki qoida qaysi manbaga asoslangani, uning dolzarbligi va xavfsizlik chegaralari tekshiriladi. AI javobi faqat Knowledge Base mavjudligi sababli avtomatik ravishda to‘g‘ri deb qabul qilinmaydi

zarur hollarda ekspert tekshiruvi va Safe Fallback mexanizmi saqlanadi. O‘zgarishlarni boshqarish: Change Request → Impact Assessment → Security/Legal Review → Test → Approval → Version Release → Monitoring → Feedback → Recalibration yoki Rollback Joriy Android prototipida ushbu barcha Production darajasidagi versiya boshqaruvi, model monitoringi va rollback mexanizmlari to‘liq ishga tushirilgan deb da’vo qilinmaydi. Mazkur model keyingi MVP/Pilot/Production bosqichlarida bosqichma-bosqich joriy etilishi kerak. Asosiy tamoyil: “Har bir muhim risk qoidasi, bilim bazasi va model o‘zgarishi versiyalangan, testlangan, tasdiqlangan va kuzatiladigan bo‘lishi kerak.” 4.10.1. Release va Change Managementning evidence-based modeli Risk qoidasi, Knowledge Base, API schema, xavfsizlik konfiguratsiyasi yoki asosiy modul o‘zgarganda o‘zgarishning ta’siri oldindan baholanadi. “Kichik o‘zgarish” deb atalgan modifikatsiya ham risk, privacy yoki integration oqimiga ta’sir qilishi mumkin. Change lifecycle: [Change Request] → [Impact Assessment] → [Security/Privacy Review] → [Development] → [Unit/Regression Test] → [Integration Test] → [Approval] → [Release] → [Monitoring] → [Rollback if Needed] → [Closure Evidence]. Backward compatibility va version pinning integratsiyalarning uzilib qolishini kamaytirish uchun qo‘llanadi

Muhim o‘zgarishlar oldingi versiyaga qaytish imkoniyati bilan chiqariladi. Har bir release uchun version, scope, test evidence, approver, deployment time va rollback plan qayd etiladi. Risk indikatorlari, qoidalar, model versiyasi, Knowledge Base va API versiyalari o‘zgarishi nazorat qilinadi: tahlil → test → xavfsizlik/compliance ko‘rib chiqishi → tasdiqlash → versiyalash → monitoring. Muhim o‘zgarishlarda backward compatibility, rollback va audit izi saqlanadi. Joriy prototipdagi bilim qatlamining mavjudligi Production model boshqaruvi allaqachon to‘liq ishlayotganini anglatmaydi. 4.11. Privileged Access, Insider Risk va Incident Response chuqurlashtirilgan modeli FINZANJIR Productionga o‘tganda platformaning o‘zidan keladigan xavf ham alohida boshqariladi. Administrator yoki yuqori vakolatli foydalanuvchining noto‘g‘ri harakati, credential o‘g‘irlanishi, secret/key sizib chiqishi yoki audit dalilini o‘zgartirishga urinish oddiy “cyberattack”dan alohida nazorat qilinadi. Nazorat zanjiri: [Least Privilege] → [MFA] → [PAM/JIT access] → [RBAC] → [Separation of Duties] → [Command/Change approval] → [Immutable/append-only audit] → [Monitoring] → [Alert] → [Containment] → [Investigation] → [Recovery] → [Post-incident review]

Breach holatida maqsad faqat tizimni tezda qayta yoqish emas: dalilni saqlash, ta’sir doirasini aniqlash, zararlangan credentiallarni bekor qilish, xizmatni xavfsiz tiklash, tegishli vakolatli tomonlarga xabar berish va post-incident corrective actionni qayd qilishdir. 4.12. RTO/RPO va Disaster Recovery targetlarini tasdiqlash modeli FINZANJIRning Pilot va kelajakdagi Production bosqichlarida muhim xizmatlar uzilishi yoki texnik hodisa yuz berganda tizimni tiklash talablari oldindan belgilanishi kerak. Bunda RTO (Recovery Time Objective), RPO (Recovery Point Objective) va Disaster Recovery (DR) talablari xizmatning muhimligi, ma’lumotlarning ahamiyati va operatsion ehtiyojlardan kelib chiqib aniqlanadi. Asosiy tasdiqlash zanjiri: Service Criticality → Maximum Tolerable Downtime → Maximum Tolerable Data Loss → RTO/RPO taklifi → DR Architecture → Recovery Test → Rahbariyat/Bank tasdig‘i → Production Gate RTO RTO (Recovery Time Objective) — xizmat yoki tizim komponenti uzilganidan keyin uni qabul qilinadigan darajada qayta tiklash uchun belgilangan maqsadli vaqt. RTO har bir xizmat uchun bir xil bo‘lishi shart emas. Muhimligi yuqori bo‘lgan xizmatlar uchun tiklanish talabi boshqacha, ikkilamchi xizmatlar uchun esa boshqa bo‘lishi mumkin. RPO RPO (Recovery Point Objective) — hodisa yuz berganda qancha vaqt oralig‘idagi ma’lumot yo‘qolishi mumkinligini belgilovchi tiklash maqsadi

RPO ma’lumotlarning biznes va operatsion ahamiyati, backup mexanizmi, replikatsiya va boshqa texnik imkoniyatlar bilan bog‘liq holda belgilanadi. Disaster Recovery Disaster Recovery modeli quyidagi holatlarni hisobga olishi mumkin: - asosiy servis yoki infratuzilmaning ishlamay qolishi; - ma’lumotlar bazasi yoki storage nosozligi; - tarmoq yoki integratsiya uzilishi; - konfiguratsiya yoki release xatosi; - kiberhodisa; - backupdan tiklash zarurati; - asosiy muhitdan zaxira muhitga o‘tish; - tiklangan tizimni qayta tekshirish. DR jarayoni faqat hujjatda mavjud bo‘lishi bilan cheklanmaydi. Zarur bo‘lganda backup va recovery mexanizmlari nazoratli test orqali tekshirilishi kerak. Recovery zanjiri: Incident → Detection → Severity → Containment → Recovery Decision → Backup/Replica → Restore/Failover → Validation → Service Recovery → Monitoring → Lessons Learned RTO/RPO va DR targetlari joriy Android prototipidan kelib chiqib taxminiy raqamlar bilan belgilanmaydi. Ular Pilot talablari, xizmatning muhimlik darajasi, infratuzilma arxitekturasi, backup/replikatsiya imkoniyatlari, capacity testlari va real recovery sinovlari asosida shakllantiriladi. Tasdiqlangan targetlar keyinchalik SLA/SLO, Operational Runbook, Incident Response va Production Gate mezonlari bilan bog‘lanishi mumkin

Asosiy tamoyil: “RTO/RPO raqami taxmin qilinmaydi — xizmat muhimligi, texnik imkoniyat va recovery testi asosida asoslanadi va tasdiqlanadi.” Joriy prototip RTO/RPO va Production darajasidagi Disaster Recovery talablari to‘liq sinovdan o‘tgan tizim sifatida ko‘rsatilmaydi. Ushbu model keyingi MVP/Pilot/Production bosqichlarida tegishli texnik, xavfsizlik va boshqaruv talablari asosida ishlab chiqiladi. 4.13. Performance, capacity va scalability boshqaruvi FINZANJIR tizimi Pilot va kelajakdagi Production bosqichlarida turli yuklama sharoitlarida barqaror ishlashi uchun performance, capacity va scalability masalalari alohida boshqarilishi kerak. Ushbu yo‘nalishning maqsadi tizimning javob berish tezligi, bir vaqtning o‘zida qayta ishlashi mumkin bo‘lgan yuklama, resurslardan foydalanishi va yuklama oshganda tizimni kengaytirish imkoniyatlarini aniqlashdan iborat. Asosiy boshqaruv zanjiri: Expected Load → Peak Load → Concurrency → Latency Target → Capacity Test → Bottleneck → Scale → Retest → Acceptance Asosiy tushunchalar Performance — tizimning so‘rov yoki operatsiyalarga qanchalik tez va barqaror javob berishini ifodalaydi. Capacity — tizim ma’lum infratuzilma va konfiguratsiya sharoitida qancha yuklamani barqaror qayta ishlay olishini aniqlaydi. Scalability — yuklama oshganda tizim resurslarini kengaytirish orqali xizmat sifatini saqlab qolish imkoniyatini bildiradi

Sinov yo‘nalishlari Pilot yoki Production oldidan zarur bo‘lsa quyidagi sinovlar o‘tkazilishi mumkin: - Baseline test — odatiy yuklama sharoitidagi ishlashni aniqlash; - Peak load test — yuqori yuklama sharoitini tekshirish; - Concurrency test — bir vaqtning o‘zida ko‘plab so‘rovlar kelgandagi holatni baholash; - Sustained load test — uzoq vaqt davomida barqaror ishlashni tekshirish; - Burst test — qisqa vaqt ichida keskin yuklama oshishini tekshirish; - Recovery after overload — ortiqcha yuklamadan keyin tizimning normal holatga qaytishini tekshirish; - Dependency degradation test — tashqi servis yoki integratsiya sekinlashganda yoki vaqtincha ishlamaganda tizimning xatti-harakatini tekshirish. Sinovlarda kamida quyidagi ko‘rsatkichlar kuzatilishi mumkin: - response time va latency; - throughput; - concurrency; - CPU va memory utilization; - API error rate; - timeout va retry holatlari; - queue yoki navbatlarning o‘sishi; - dependency response time; - tiklanish vaqti; - resurslardan foydalanish dinamikasi. Aniq Production capacity, latency yoki throughput raqamlari joriy prototipdan kelib chiqib o‘zboshimchalik bilan belgilanmaydi. Ular Pilot talablari, realistik yuklama modeli, infratuzilma konfiguratsiyasi, capacity testlari va qabul mezonlari asosida aniqlanadi

Agar test natijasida bottleneck aniqlansa, uning sababi tahlil qilinadi va zarur bo‘lsa arxitektura, konfiguratsiya, ma’lumotlar bazasi, API, queue yoki boshqa tegishli komponentlar optimallashtiriladi. Keyinchalik test qayta o‘tkazilib, o‘zgarishning natijasi tasdiqlanadi. Performance boshqaruvi sikli: Measure → Analyze → Identify Bottleneck → Optimize/Scale → Retest → Monitor Joriy Android prototipi Production darajasidagi performance, capacity yoki scalability sinovlaridan to‘liq o‘tgan deb da’vo qilinmaydi. Ushbu bo‘lim kelajakdagi MVP/Pilot/Production bosqichlarida bajarilishi kerak bo‘lgan texnik boshqaruv va sinov talablarini belgilaydi. Asosiy tamoyil: “Yuklama oshishini taxmin qilishning o‘zi yetarli emas — yuklama o‘lchanadi, bottleneck aniqlanadi, tizim kengaytiriladi va qayta sinovdan o‘tkaziladi.” 4.14. Platforma bo‘yicha Threat Modeling Threat modeling FINZANJIRning faqat bitta modulini emas, butun ma’lumot oqimini ko‘rib chiqadi. Har bir muhim asset, trust boundary, external dependency va privileged action uchun ehtimoliy tahdidlar aniqlanadi. Model: [Asset] → [Trust Boundary] → [Threat/Attack Path] → [Existing Control] → [Residual Risk] → [Owner] → [Test] → [Mitigation] → [Retest] → [Accepted/Unresolved Risk]

Asosiy aktivlar: bank/PSP exchange, identity, Case evidence, audit logs, Risk Engine rules, Knowledge Base, credentials/keys, backups va administrative interfaces. Threat modeling natijasi Dependency/Risk Register va Production Gate bilan bog‘lanadi. Kritik unresolved risk mavjud bo‘lsa, tegishli gate HOLD yoki CONDITIONAL holatiga o‘tishi mumkin. FINZANJIR real banklararo muhitga o‘tganda faqat funksional to‘g‘rilik yetarli bo‘lmaydi. Tizimning yuklama ostidagi xatti-harakati, navbatlar, API latency, parallel so‘rovlar, storage va graph query yuklamasi oldindan o‘lchanadi. Capacity planning modeli: [Expected Load] → [Peak Load] → [Concurrency] → [Latency Target] → [Capacity Test] → [Bottleneck Analysis] → [Scale-up/Scale-out] → [Retest] → [Acceptance]. Aniq Production hajmlari hozircha o‘ylab topilmaydi. Ular pilot banklarning real yoki sintetik yuklama profili, TT va SLA talablari asosida belgilanadi. Testlar: baseline, peak load, sustained load, burst load, recovery after overload va dependency degradation. Dalil: load-test report, latency distribution, error rate, resource utilization va capacity recommendation. Hozirgi hujjatda RTO/RPO uchun yakuniy Production raqamlarini ixtiro qilmaymiz

i, bank bilan kelishilgan SLA/SLO, ma’lumot yo‘qotishning maqbul chegarasi, backup arxitekturasi va pilot/DR test natijalari asosida ekspertlar bilan tasdiqlanadi. Targetni belgilash zanjiri: [Service criticality] → [Maximum tolerable downtime] → [Maximum tolerable data loss] → [RTO/RPO proposal] → [Architecture cost] → [Restore test] → [Management/Bank approval] → [Production Gate]. 5-bob. Biznes modeli va moliyaviy barqarorlik ... 5.1. Tijoratlashtirish maqsadi FINZANJIRning amaliy qiymati: bank va PSP ichidagi mavjud nazoratlarni almashtirmasdan, turli ruxsat etilgan signallarni yagona tahlil kontekstiga keltirish, tekshirilishi kerak bo‘lgan holatni Casega aylantirish, auditni yaxshilash va hodisadan keyingi javobni tezroq muvofiqlashtirishga ko‘maklashish. Tijoriy model shu funksional qiymatni texnik xizmat, integratsiya, monitoring va xavfsizlik xarajatlarini barqaror qoplash bilan bog‘laydi. Tijoratlashtirishning maqsadi xavfsizlik vazifasini tijoriy manfaatga almashtirish emas. Maqsad — platformaning uzoq muddatli ekspluatatsiya, texnik xizmat, xavfsizlik monitoringi, yangilanish va kengayish xarajatlarini barqaror qoplash mexanizmini yaratish. 5.2

lari va fintech kompaniyalari Elektron to‘lov/raqamli xizmat ko‘rsatuvchi tashkilotlar Korporativ mijozlar Davlat va tegishli vakolatli tashkilotlar bilan kelishilgan loyihalar Xalqaro texnologik va moliyaviy xavfsizlik hamkorlari 5.3. Daromad oqimlari Antifraud/risk monitoring xizmat haqi 24/7 SOC va xavfsizlik monitoringi API/integratsiya ulash va qo‘llab-quvvatlash xizmatlari Platforma litsenziyasi yoki SaaS modeli Audit, xavfsizlik tekshiruvi va pentest xizmatlari FIN-RECOVERY/tezkor javob koordinatsiyasi bo‘yicha xizmatlar Boshqa tashkilotlar uchun joriy etish, sozlash va texnik qo‘llab-quvvatlash 5.4. 12 oylik indikativ ishchi model Moliyaviy modelning hisoblash farazi: 17.415 mlrd so‘mlik summa tayyor tijoriy narx emas, balki resurslar, infratuzilma, 24/7 operatsiya, audit, integratsiya, pilot va zaxira xarajatlarini dastlabki rejalashtirish uchun tuzilgan indikativ modeldir. Har bir asosiy band keyingi texnik topshiriqda miqdor, birlik narxi, muddat va yetkazib beruvchi takliflari bilan qayta hisoblanadi. Ekspert uchun tekshiriladigan moliyaviy dalil modeli: CAPEX → OPEX → xizmat hajmi → birlik xarajat → tarif/kontrakt → daromad → break-even/operatsion barqarorlik. Shuning uchun 17.415 mlrd so‘mning o‘zi “daromad” yoki “MVP narxi” deb talqin qilinmaydi. Quyidagi raqamlar yakuniy tijoriy taklif emas
